name: Jilly Juice

card.summary: A homemade fermented cabbage-and-salt drink promoted online as a detox for skin, gut and body, taken in large daily amounts by its followers.
card.note: Very high sodium; dehydration and salt-intoxication risks have been raised by physicians; regulators have warned about its health claims.

quick.overview:
Jilly Juice is a homemade drink of fermented cabbage, water and salt created by Jillian Epperly and spread through Facebook groups from 2017. Followers drink it in the belief that it clears Candida and parasites and leaves the body, gut and skin cleaner.

The appearance angle is the 'detox' idea: followers describe clearer skin and a leaner, healthier look as by-products of gut cleansing. No clinical trials have tested the drink, and physicians who commented in the press have raised safety concerns.
quick.how: Proponents describe shredding cabbage, mixing it with salt and water and letting it ferment at room temperature for a few days. Followers then drink it daily, building up from a small volume, alongside a restricted diet, and describe loose stools as the sign the protocol is working.
quick.risks: Doctors quoted in news coverage point to the high salt content, dehydration and hypernatremia (salt intoxication) as risks, plus possible harm from poorly fermented batches. The FTC warned Epperly in 2018 that health claims need scientific support. Anyone on medication or with a medical condition is advised by clinicians to consult a doctor.

lead: Jilly Juice is a homemade fermented drink made from cabbage (sometimes kale), water and salt, created by Jillian Mai Thi Epperly of Ohio. She began making it in October 2016 and posted about it on Facebook from January 2017 [3][1].

Followers drink it as a gut 'detox' and describe wider benefits including clearer skin, weight change and a healthier appearance; Epperly herself claimed far broader effects, from curing autism and cancer to regrowing limbs and reversing aging [3][1]. She teaches that Candida and parasites underlie many illnesses and that the drink removes them, with the resulting diarrhea (followers' 'waterfalls') read as evidence of clearing [3].

No clinical studies have tested Jilly Juice. Physicians quoted in the press, including Joseph Schwarcz of McGill University and David Seres of Columbia University Medical Center, have warned about its salt content and dehydration risk [3]. The drink drew national attention after an appearance on Dr. Phil in May 2018 and an FTC warning the same year [3].

chain: Claimed result: clearer skin, leaner, healthier look
angle.text: Followers use it as a gut cleanse and report expecting clearer skin and a healthier look as downstream effects. The appearance benefit is a claim made by proponents; it has not been tested.

paras: The drink is cabbage fermented in a salt brine at room temperature, similar to sauerkraut juice; proponents say it ferments for about three days [3][1]. Epperly recommended starting at about two cups a day and increasing the amount over time, and followers combine it with a simple diet [3][1].

Epperly, an Ohio insurance agent with no medical training, turned to alternative health after a diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder and began fermenting cabbage in late 2016 [3]. A Facebook group grew past 58,000 members; in February 2017 she launched a paid website and offered paid consultations [3].
Coverage in 2018, including Newsweek and a May 2018 Dr. Phil episode on which host Phil McGraw called the claims 'outrageous', brought it to a wide audience [3].

Epperly and followers hold that Candida overgrowth and parasites cause many conditions and that the juice removes them through the bowels. Claims have included curing autism, cancer and psoriasis, reversing aging and regenerating tissue [3][1]. Followers inspect stool as proof of detoxification [1].
No studies found. No trial has tested the drink for skin, weight or any other outcome.

The recipe is not approved by the FDA. Physicians have said dehydration and salt intoxication are possible risks, that the high salt may raise blood pressure, and that poor fermentation could cause harm [3]. Reported symptoms in the protocol include diarrhea, cramping, vomiting and fatigue, which followers attribute to detox [1].

In 2017 Bruce Wilmot, who had metastatic pancreatic cancer, died about a month after starting the drink; his daughter said he drank so much he was effectively starving himself, while Epperly said he did not drink enough [3]. In 2018 the FTC warned Epperly that health claims require adequate scientific support, and critics filed complaints with several agencies [3].

timeline.event: Epperly begins making the drink in October [3]
Facebook videos and group; paid website launched in February [3]
Dr. Phil appearance (May) and FTC warning [3]

lore.intro: The drink is discussed mainly in wellness and detox communities; its appearance claims are secondary to the gut-cleanse narrative [1].

claims.claim: Drinking it clears parasites and Candida from the body
claims.believers: Followers interpret loose stools and stool appearance as expelled parasites and biofilm [1].
claims.experts: Physicians quoted in the press say the claims are unsupported and that the drink carries dehydration and salt risks [3].

claims.claim: It can cure serious disease and reverse aging
claims.believers: Epperly has said it can cure autism and cancer and regenerate tissue [3].
claims.experts: The FDA has not approved it, no studies support the claims, and the FTC warned about unsupported health claims [3].
